source.title: MAAT: Multi-phase Adapter-Aware Targeted Unlearning
source.authors: S. Yagnik; Shubham Gaur; Saksham Thakur; Vinija Jain; Aman Chadha; Amitava Das

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates forgetting and retention with a balanced question benchmark and FSR/RSR measures, but does not test recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports unlearning outcomes for MAAT and baselines. Its citations to relearning attacks and other unlearning work are not this study's results. It does not run a relearning attack, activation-direction ablation, quantization attack, or prompting-only recovery test.
record.test_reason: In a new setting, the study reports whether several unlearning methods remove implanted facts while keeping other implanted facts. It uses LoRA-implanted Factify facts on a balanced 5W benchmark with an LLM judge. This bears on the efficacy half of A. It runs no recovery attack, so B–F and A's attack-resistance part are untested. MAAT does not claim robustness, so F is not engaged.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that existing baselines trade forgetting against retention on Why-type causal facts. They claim MAAT is the first method to exceed 60% FSR and 60% RSR on all five categories on LLaMA 3.2-3B. They attribute its weaker Gemma results to architecture-dependent separability. In the limitations they call for adversarial paraphrase probing to check whether unlearning is genuine or merely suppresses recall.
record.recipe_differences: M AAT is a three-phase LoRA adapter unlearning method using projected ascent, adapter-rank pruning, task-vector negation, and retain repair. It evaluates GA and GA+KL baselines, but does not reproduce or test the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model architecture and question category. The paper reports lower aggregate M AAT FSR/RSR on Gemma 3-4B than on LLaMA 3.2-3B and different outcomes across 5W categories.

fits_no_version.finding: In the ablation (LLaMA, 200 samples), upgrading the method's own retain-set repair phase lowered FSR from 48% to 43%. Forget ROUGE-1 rose from 0.520 to 0.614; the authors say repair 'inadvertently recovers forgotten content'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign retain-set repair fine-tuning inside an unlearning pipeline can partly restore forgotten facts. This is method-internal, not an attack.

record.code_released: The authors say code is publicly available; no URL is stated.
record.problems: Evaluation uses a single Qwen 2.5-7B judge, covers two model families at 3–4B scale, and reports no uncertainty estimates. The paper itself notes the need for adversarial paraphrase probing.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed category-by-category values in Table 3, TOFU results in Table 4, and ablation-condition results in Appendix A are not extracted here; the selected rows capture aggregate and Why-type results relevant to the tested unlearning-performance portion of version A. The reported ablations compare components of the proposed unlearning procedure, not the recovery attacks in versions B–E.

untested.parts: Resistance to simple attacks (relearning, paraphrase, jailbreak, quantization). Chance-level comparison. General-capability benchmarks beyond implanted retain facts. The authors themselves defer paraphrase probing.
No relearning or fine-tuning recovery attack.
No activation-direction ablation or access-vs-deletion analysis. The Appendix F encoding analysis concerns where facts are stored, not recovery.
No quantization of unlearned weights. 4-bit NF4 is used only during implantation.
No prompting recovery. Rephrases exist in the benchmark, but rephrase augmentation is disabled and no paraphrase evaluation is reported.
MAAT is not tested against, and does not claim to resist, recovery attacks.

missing.what: Gemma 3-4B baseline aggregates: GA 61.2/51.0, GA+KL 42.8/61.6, AN 82.0/25.0, RO-FT 51.4/70.4 (FSR/RSR).
TOFU forget05 FSR/RSR for all methods, e.g. MAAT LLaMA 67.0/46.6, AN 100/0.2. Declared left out, but needed for cross-study comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The forget and retain sets are both LoRA-implanted facts, and the adapter is never merged. Results are from a single Qwen 2.5-7B judge with no uncertainty reported. There is no chance baseline because the evaluation is open-ended. The study never examines whether 'forgotten' facts are recoverable, so it says nothing about shallowness itself.

versions.untested_parts: Attack resistance is not tested. The study reports FSR/RSR, not an explicit comparison to chance-level targeted accuracy.
No recovery fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or test of access-blocking versus deletion is reported.
No quantization attack on unlearned weights is tested. The paper's 4-bit quantization is used during knowledge implantation.
No prompting-only recovery via rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information is tested. Rephrase augmentation is disabled in the reported M AAT settings.
The study does not test whether M AAT resists the recovery attacks listed in the claim.

rows.subject: LLaMA 3.2-3B
rows.operation_detail: M AAT unlearning evaluated by LLM-judge FSR on 5WB ENCH aggregate forget split
rows.note: FSR is the rate at which the judge finds the ground truth absent; this is not a reported chance-level accuracy.
rows.check: No pre-unlearning FSR baseline is reported (only implantation ROUGE, Table 5). 22.6% of forget facts are still produced without any attack, which is not near-chance.

relationships.condition: MAAT on 5WBench, LLaMA 3.2-3B and Gemma 3-4B (aggregate and Why-type)
relationships.reason: Forgetting is incomplete even without attacks: FSR 77.4%/64.0% and Why-FSR 63%/55%. Retention of implanted facts is only 61.8–71.6% (r1–r4, r13–r16).
relationships.display_finding: FSR reached 77.4%/64.0% and Why-FSR 63%/55%, while retention of implanted facts remained only 61.8–71.6%.

relationships.condition: GA and GA+KL baselines on LLaMA 3.2-3B
relationships.reason: Retention is high only where forgetting is weak: GA FSR 57.4%, GA+KL FSR 33.8%, GA+KL Why-FSR 22% with 93% RSR (r7–r10, r17–r20).
relationships.display_finding: GA and GA+KL achieved FSR of 57.4% and 33.8%; GA+KL retained 93% RSR but reached only 22% Why-FSR.

relationships.condition: Adapter Negation and RO-FT baselines on LLaMA 3.2-3B
relationships.reason: AN reaches 99.8% FSR only with RSR 0.4%. RO-FT matches MAAT's FSR but keeps only 35.2% RSR. Forgetting costs retention (r5, r6, r11, r12).
relationships.display_finding: Adapter Negation achieved 99.8% FSR with only 0.4% RSR, while RO-FT matched MAAT's FSR but retained only 35.2% RSR.
